records.sourceFile: Quantifying Muscle Volume Deficits Among 38 Lower Extremity Muscles in Collegiate Football Athletes After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.pdf

paper.citation: Ito N, Martin JA, Joachim MR, Blemker SS, Opar DA, Kliethermes SA, et al. Quantifying Muscle Volume Deficits Among 38 Lower Extremity Muscles in Collegiate Football Athletes After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction. Am J Sports Med. 2025.
paper.abstract: Quadriceps dysfunction is common after ACL reconstruction (ACLR). This exploratory cross-sectional study used MRI with machine-learning segmentation to quantify volume deficits across 38 lower extremity muscles in 30 male Division I football athletes after primary unilateral ACLR. The largest deficits were in the uniarticular quadriceps, followed by the gastrocnemii. The fibularis group was larger in the surgical limb, and most other muscles showed no difference between limbs.
paper.tldr: In collegiate football players about two years after ACL reconstruction and back to full play, quadriceps volume remained lower on the surgical side. Gastrocnemius volume was also lower, which suggests plantarflexor work deserves consideration.
paper.methods: Secondary analysis of a prospective cohort of Division I football athletes with primary unilateral ACLR and lower extremity MRI at full participation. Volumes were segmented automatically from 3-T MRI, normalized to body weight and height, converted to Z scores, and compared between limbs with paired t tests, with a forest plot ranking muscles by standardized mean difference. A separate analysis excluded hamstring autografts (n = 25).
paper.findings: The three uniarticular quadriceps muscles showed the largest surgical-limb deficits, and the biarticular rectus femoris showed a similar deficit that was not significant. The medial and lateral gastrocnemii were lower in the surgical limb, while the soleus was not. The combined fibularis muscles were greater in the surgical limb. Semitendinosus did not differ overall (mean difference -0.15 mL/kg/m, 95% CI -0.32 to 0.02, P = .080). Across athletes, vasti volume symmetry was positively associated with time from surgery (R2 0.19 to 0.49), but rectus femoris and gastrocnemius symmetry were not.
paper.limitations: Cross-sectional design, so causation and change over time cannot be inferred. Small single-team sample with no power analysis and many comparisons, so some findings (notably the fibularis result) may be type I errors and null results may be type II errors. Muscle volume was not paired with strength or function measures.
paper.practicalImplications: Quadriceps volume deficits were still present in high-level athletes who had returned to sport, which supports keeping isolated quadriceps strengthening in rehabilitation and beyond. The gastrocnemius deficit suggests that isolated plantarflexion strengthening could be considered, but this study does not show that it changes outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: Quadriceps volume deficits persisted for years in returned-to-play collegiate players, so strength plans should keep the quadriceps as a priority. The study did not test whether training closes these deficits.
paper.rtp: The study shows that muscle volume asymmetries can persist after athletes return to full participation. It cannot establish readiness to return to sport, because it did not link the deficits to re-injury or performance.

records.sourceFile: Questioning the rules of engagement - A critical analysis of the use of limb symmetry index for safe return to sport after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.pdf

paper.citation: Simonsson R, Sundberg A, Piussi R, Högberg J, Senorski C, Thomeé R, et al. Questioning the rules of engagement: a critical analysis of the use of limb symmetry index for safe return to sport after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. Br J Sports Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: This observational cohort study used Project ACL registry data from 233 athletes aged 15 to 30 years with a pre-injury Tegner score of 6 or higher after ACL reconstruction. Limb symmetry index (LSI) from knee strength and three hop tests was evaluated against a safe return to sport, defined as no second ACL injury within 2 years. LSI cut-offs, continuous LSI and deviation from symmetry did not reliably differentiate athletes with a safe return from those without, although 80% or 85% LSI on all tests was associated with lower odds of a safe return.
paper.tldr: In young athletes after ACL reconstruction, limb symmetry index from strength and hop tests did not reliably separate those who returned to sport safely from those who had a second ACL injury within 2 years. LSI should be one part of return-to-sport decisions, not the only one.
paper.methods: Observational cohort using prospectively collected data from the Project ACL rehabilitation registry in Gothenburg. Athletes aged 15 to 30 with pre-injury Tegner of 6 or higher and a completed muscle function test battery at return to sport were included. LSI was tested with ROC and AUC for best cut-offs, with logistic regression for predefined cut-offs (80% to 90%), for each 1% increment in LSI, and for deviation from 100% symmetry. Outcome was a second ACL injury within 2 years of return.
paper.findings: Of 233 athletes, 37 (16%) had a second ACL injury within 2 years of return. Best-differentiating LSI cut-offs had poor discrimination (AUC 0.50 to 0.59; the vertical hop cut-off was significant at P = .04 but had no useful discrimination). Meeting 80% LSI on all tests (OR 0.32, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.87) or 85% (OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.84) was associated with lower odds of a safe return, with poor AUCs of 0.60 to 0.61. Meeting 90% was not significant (OR 0.65). Each 1% change in LSI or in deviation from symmetry had no significant association with a safe return, except the vertical hop LSI (OR 0.97 per 1%, P = .04).
paper.limitations: Return to sport was defined by a self-rated Tegner score recorded only at scheduled follow-ups, so the true return date may differ and the rating does not show training exposure. Concomitant cartilage and meniscal injuries were not recorded, second injuries were self-reported, and absolute limb values were not considered. The abstract reports no effect of a 1% increase in LSI, while Table 1 shows a significant vertical hop association (P = .04); the authors note the cut-offs require replication in another cohort.
paper.practicalImplications: LSI from knee strength and hop tests should not be the only basis for clearing an athlete to return to sport. The study does not show a cut-off that identifies a safe return, so LSI results should sit alongside time since surgery, psychological readiness and other measures. The finding that 80% or 85% LSI on all tests was linked to lower odds of a safe return should be treated as a weak signal with poor discrimination.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the study does not support using a single LSI score to predict who is ready to play. Strength and hop testing can still help track progress and motivation, but the results do not identify which athletes will avoid a second ACL injury.
paper.rtp: The study addresses return-to-sport testing directly and finds that LSI cut-offs from strength and hop tests cannot reliably separate athletes with a safe return from those who later re-injure. It cannot be used to certify a safe return to sport on LSI alone, and it does not show that any particular test battery is sufficient for clearance.

records.sourceFile: Ramping isometrics for accelerated return to play following hamstring tendon repair - A case study.pdf

paper.citation: Power D, Haddad F, Wallis S, Baar K. Ramping Isometrics for Accelerated Return to Play following Hamstring Tendon Repair: A Case Study. Journal of Elite Sport Performance. 2023.
paper.abstract: This case study describes an elite international rugby union player with a retracted semimembranosus tear, combined with biceps femoris and semitendinosus injury, treated with surgical repair. The authors used a low-jerk ramping isometric protocol early in rehabilitation, alongside progressive loading and nutrition support. The player returned to team training at 10 weeks, returned to play at 12 weeks after surgery, and had no reinjury over the following two seasons.
paper.tldr: One elite rugby player returned to play 12 weeks after a surgically repaired semimembranosus tear, using early ramped isometrics within a bundled rehabilitation and nutrition plan. This single case shows the protocol was tolerated without reinjury, not that it speeds recovery.
paper.methods: Clinical case description of one player's post-surgical rehabilitation. Isometric loading began in the first session as 5-second ramps, a 20-second hold and a 5-second release, with a load sensor and phone app used for feedback. Strength was tracked with isometric heel-dig tests on a force platform and Nordic eccentric tests, and MRI was repeated at 8 weeks after surgery.
paper.findings: Nordic eccentric strength improved steadily with exposure; a 17.5% eccentric limb symmetry deficit remained at week 9 and the player returned to training with a 14% eccentric deficit. The authors report absolute eccentric strength above pre-injury baseline at return to play, and a between-limb imbalance they describe as moderate. Over the 16-week period, the summed eight skinfolds fell by 18.6 mm and body mass by 0.9 kg, and high-speed running distances after return were above pre-injury levels.
paper.limitations: This is a single uncontrolled case, and the protocol was one part of a multimodal program, so no effect of the isometric protocol can be isolated. The authors note that eccentric tests after running were fatigued, and that the isometric and eccentric results did not agree.
paper.practicalImplications: This case supports discussing early, pain-free ramped isometric loading with the surgeon after proximal hamstring tendon repair, with close monitoring of symptoms and tendon status. It does not establish a standard timeline, and the isometric dose and ramp rate should not be assumed to transfer to other injuries.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The case shows a staged progression from isometrics to eccentric, reactive and high-speed work, with Nordic and isometric tests tracked as limb symmetry. Running was built from partial body-weight treadmill sessions to pitch-based high-speed running with GPS-based targets.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The 12-week return came from one player who passed the other criteria and still had a 14% eccentric deficit. It cannot set a return timeline for other players or injury grades, and it cannot show that ramped isometrics shorten recovery. Reinjury data cover only the two seasons reported.

records.sourceFile: Reasons for not returning to pre-injury sport level after ACL reconstruction.pdf

paper.citation: Bashaireh KM, Yabroudi MA, Logerstedt D, Snyder-Mackler L, Nawasreh ZH. Reasons for Not Returning to Pre-injury Sport Level After ACL-Reconstruction. Int J Sports Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: The study surveyed athletes about 2 years after hamstring-autograft ACL reconstruction to find whether they had returned to their pre-injury sport level and, if not, why, and which factors were linked to the main reasons. Only 10% of the 91 athletes had returned to their pre-injury level. Lack of confidence or fear of re-injury and post-surgical knee impairment were the most common reasons, and knee giving-way was the only significant predictor of knee impairment.
paper.tldr: Only 10% of 91 athletes had returned to their pre-injury sport level two years after hamstring-graft ACL reconstruction. Fear of re-injury, low confidence and knee impairment were the main reasons given, and giving-way episodes were the only factor tied to ongoing knee impairment.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional survey of athletes aged 14 to 50 who had a primary hamstring-autograft ACL reconstruction 1 to 5 years earlier and played level I or II sports, carried out between July 2017 and August 2018. Athletes completed a self-administered questionnaire on pre-injury sport, return to sport, knee giving-way and second knee injuries, and chose and ranked reasons for not returning, with injuries confirmed by MRI and surgical reports. Univariate logistic regression tested predictors of the two most common reasons.
paper.findings: Nine of 91 athletes (10%; 95% CI 4.6 to 17.9%) had returned to their pre-injury level at a mean follow-up of 1.8 years. Among the 82 who gave reasons, lack of confidence or fear of re-injury was most common (56 athletes, 68.3%), followed by post-surgical knee impairment (43 athletes, 52.4%), and little time or work and family obligations (each 23.2%). Knee giving-way was the only significant predictor of knee impairment as a reason (OR 8.3, 95% CI 2.48 to 27.42, p = 0.001), and no variable significantly predicted fear or lack of confidence.
paper.limitations: The cross-sectional, self-report design carries recall bias, and about 30% of eligible athletes did not respond or were lost, although the authors found no demographic differences. Only two women took part, so results cannot be generalised to women, and rehabilitation was not standardised. Knee giving-way was not confirmed by clinical tests or MRI, and the sample is small. The abstract reports 48.8% and 39% for the two main reasons, which are the shares naming each as the only or primary reason; the Results values for any mention (68.3% and 52.4%) are reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: Rehabilitation should check fear, confidence and knee impairment, for example by assessing psychological status, explaining expected timelines and gradually exposing athletes to higher knee demands. Athletes who report giving-way should have dynamic knee stability addressed before high-demand sport, and their own view of knee impairment should be asked about during rehabilitation.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Reported giving-way was tied to ongoing knee impairment, so performance staff should watch for it during return-to-training and build dynamic knee stability work before high-demand sessions. Fear and low confidence were the leading reasons athletes had not returned, and the authors suggest addressing them with psychological checks and graded exposure.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study explains why athletes 1 to 5 years after reconstruction had not returned, so it can guide which psychological and knee-stability items to check before clearance. It did not identify criteria that predict return, and it cannot show that addressing these reasons raises return rates.

records.sourceFile: Recommendations for hamstring function recovery after ACL reconstruction.pdf

paper.citation: Buckthorpe M, Danelon F, La Rosa G, Nanni G, Stride M, Della Villa F. Recommendations for Hamstring Function Recovery After ACL Reconstruction. Sports Med. 2020.
paper.abstract: The authors discuss deficits in hamstring function after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), particularly with ipsilateral hamstring autograft, and how to restore them within the functional recovery process. They cover training principles such as optimal loading, eccentric and longer-length strengthening, balance of knee- and hip-dominant exercises, functional strength, and a stage-by-stage programme. They also propose return-to-sport hamstring testing and criteria.
paper.tldr: After ACL reconstruction with a hamstring graft, knee flexor strength often stays below the other leg at return to sport and for years afterwards. The authors propose a staged hamstring programme that moves from low-load isometrics to high-speed running, and they recommend testing knee flexor strength before return to sport.
paper.methods: Narrative review and recommendation paper by a multidisciplinary group, with no systematic search described. The authors combine hamstring injury prevention and rehabilitation research, ACLR studies, and their own staged rehabilitation framework (Table 2) to set out training principles, stage goals, exercise choices and return-to-sport criteria.
paper.findings: Knee flexor strength deficits after ACLR are common and are usually 0 to 20% at return to sport, with larger deficits after hamstring tendon grafts. Reported knee flexor isometric LSI after hamstring grafts was 54%, 70% and 76% at 4, 8 and 12 weeks. The proposed training principles include periodised resistance training, eccentric and long-length work, a balance of knee-dominant and hip-dominant exercises, and high-speed running in the late stage. The recommended return-to-sport screen is a knee flexor LSI of 90% or more, a knee flexor to extensor ratio of 60% or more, and a knee flexor peak torque of 1.5 Nm/kg at 90 degrees per second.
paper.limitations: As a narrative review with no described search, the selection of evidence cannot be checked. Much of the supporting evidence comes from hamstring injury populations rather than ACLR, and the authors state that evidence is missing on several points, including whether to delay hamstring loading after graft harvest, the timing of stage transitions, and the choice of exercises in the presence of tendon regeneration problems.
paper.practicalImplications: Test knee flexor strength, and not only the standard knee extensor and hop tests, before clearing an ACLR athlete for return to sport. Progress from isometric and low-load work early, to moderate-load hypertrophy and strength work in mid stage, to high-load eccentric, long-length and high-speed running work late in the programme. Use both knee-dominant exercises, such as the Nordic hamstring exercise, and hip-dominant exercises.
paper.athleteDev: Build hamstring work into the late-stage block with heavy eccentric and long-length exercise and high-speed running, then add explosive and sport-specific work as the athlete tolerates it. Where a hamstring graft was used, balance knee-dominant and hip-dominant exercises to address both the knee flexors and the medial and lateral hamstring muscles.
paper.rtp: Use the knee flexor LSI of at least 90%, knee flexor to extensor ratio of at least 60%, and knee flexor peak torque of about 1.5 Nm/kg at 90 degrees per second as the authors' proposed screening standard, with eccentric testing (for example NordBord LSI above 90% and peak force above 350 N) where available. These thresholds are proposals, not outcomes shown to reduce re-injury, so they cannot prove an athlete is ready to return. The review cannot say whether these criteria reduce re-injury rates.

records.sourceFile: Recurrent hamstring muscle injury - Applying the limited   evidence in the professional football setting with a seven   point program.pdf

paper.citation: Brukner P, Nealon A, Morgan C, Burgess D, Dunn A. Recurrent hamstring muscle injury: applying the limited evidence in the professional football setting with a seven-point programme. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2014;48:929-938.
paper.abstract: A professional footballer with five hamstring injuries in five months was managed with a seven-part programme and returned to play at 42 days, then missed no games due to hamstring problems. The paper reviews the limited evidence for each intervention and states that which component caused the outcome cannot be determined.
paper.tldr: A single professional player with repeated hamstring injuries recovered with a multi-part programme that combined biomechanical correction, neural mobilisation, eccentric strengthening and a high-speed running overload. Clinicians should treat it as a case example, not as a tested protocol.
paper.methods: Clinical case description of one 26-year-old professional footballer with five hamstring episodes over five months. Management after the fifth episode combined orthotics for a 5 mm functional leg length difference with osteopathic manual therapy, more aggressive neural mobilisation and lumbar manual therapy, core stability work, a 1-in-3-day eccentric strength programme, an eight-cycle high-speed running overload programme tracked with GPS, local anaesthetic, Traumeel and Actovegin injections, and yoga-based stretching and relaxation. Two L4-5 epidural steroid injections had been given earlier, after the third episode and between the fourth and fifth, and the evidence base for each intervention was reviewed.
paper.findings: The player returned to full-team training 33 days and was available for selection at 39 days after the fifth episode, then returned to play at 42 days. He played 33 of 42 possible games to season end, missing seven games with a ruptured plantaris but none for hamstring problems. The overload running programme gave 49.8% more high-speed running distance than the previous standard rehabilitation, with 16.8% more training time, and the player reported subjective improvement in hamstring freedom.
paper.limitations: Single case with no control group, so no causal attribution is possible. Seven interventions were applied together, and the authors state that the key component cannot be identified. Outcomes after the return are described only as games played and absence, and the subjective improvements are self-reported. The authors note there have been no controlled trials of Actovegin or Traumeel for hamstring injury. Table 1 lists 28 days to team training and 38 days to play for episode 5, which differs from the 33 and 42 days given in the Outcome section.
paper.practicalImplications: For a recurrent hamstring injury with neural or lumbopelvic symptoms, the paper suggests assessing those factors alongside the muscle, and it describes how a high-speed running overload block was used to build running load before return. It supports individualised, multi-component management with planned monitoring, but not a fixed protocol.
paper.athleteDev: The paper describes monitoring a player's training and match running with GPS, heart rate and HRV, and using that data to shape a high-speed running overload block and conditioning. It does not test whether these methods improve performance in athletes without injury.
paper.rtp: The player returned to full training at 33 days and to play at 42 days after the fifth episode, and then had no further hamstring absence. The paper can illustrate one return-to-play pathway for a recurrent hamstring injury, but a single case cannot set return-to-play criteria or a safe timeline for other athletes.

records.sourceFile: Reframing Recovery - Fantasy sports metrics as scalable tools for measuring post-injury athletic performance.pdf

paper.citation: Gadbois WJ, Cohn H, Vaidya R. Reframing Recovery: Fantasy Sports Metrics as Scalable Tools for Measuring Post-injury Athletic Performance. Cureus. 2025;17(9):e91602.
paper.abstract: Return to play does not show whether athletes regain their pre-injury performance. This review used a targeted PubMed search to find six studies that used fantasy scores or WAR to measure post-injury performance in the NFL, NBA, MLB and NHL. Fantasy scores and WAR fell after injury in 14 of 15 sport-specific cohorts, and the authors propose them as a basis for a standardized return to pre-injury performance (RPIP) measure.
paper.tldr: Across six small studies of professional North American athletes, fantasy scores and WAR usually dropped after injury. Staff can use them as a candidate performance outcome alongside return to play, but not yet as a validated measure.
paper.methods: Narrative review with a targeted PubMed search for studies using fantasy scores or WAR to measure post-injury performance in the four major North American leagues. Studies were required to stratify by injury type and use publicly available scoring data. Six studies met criteria, and each was appraised with the STROBE checklist.
paper.findings: Six studies (15 cohorts, 785 athletes) were included. Fantasy scores or WAR declined after injury in 14 of 15 cohorts, including NFL ACL cohorts where running backs and wide receivers declined (p<0.05) and NFL ankle injury cohorts (p<0.0001). The one exception was an MLB tibial fracture cohort (n=9) that improved by 8.1%. Only two studies referred to RPIP.
paper.limitations: Seven of 15 cohorts had fewer than 20 athletes. Most studies were retrospective and excluded players who retired after injury, which may underestimate declines. Few studies reported inferential statistics or effect sizes, the search was limited to PubMed, and scoring systems varied across platforms. The authors call the design narrative, although a defined search was used.
paper.practicalImplications: Fantasy scores and WAR are public, game-by-game and comparable across seasons, so they could be tracked to see whether an athlete is producing at a pre-injury level after return. Because the evidence is small and retrospective, any such use should be a supplementary check next to clinical measures.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: a player's fantasy or WAR output before and after a lower-limb or spine injury can serve as a longitudinal performance reference, but the review does not provide thresholds or benchmarks for judging readiness.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the review supports the idea that return to play does not capture performance recovery, but it cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria, clearance thresholds or expected percentage recovery, because no RPIP standard or validated cut-off exists.

records.sourceFile: Rehabilitation and return to play protocols after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in soccer players - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Mayer MA, Deliso M, Hong IS, et al. Rehabilitation and Return to Play Protocols After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in Soccer Players: A Systematic Review. Am J Sports Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: This systematic review of 23 studies (874 soccer players after ACL reconstruction) looked for rehabilitation protocols and functional tests that support return to play in soccer. The authors found no consensus, with wide heterogeneity in protocols and test batteries, return-to-play times of 3 to 8 months, and few reports of complications or long-term follow-up.
paper.tldr: Rehabilitation and return-to-play testing after ACL reconstruction in soccer lack standardization, and the evidence is small, mostly retrospective and male-dominated. Staff should document and justify their own test batteries and progression criteria rather than adopt a protocol from this review.
paper.methods: Systematic review of PubMed, Embase and CENTRAL following PRISMA, with two independent reviewers for selection and data extraction. Original studies at level of evidence 1 to 4 that reported rehabilitation protocols, knee rehabilitation metrics or clinical outcomes in soccer players after ACL reconstruction were included. Non-randomized studies were appraised with MINORS and the two RCTs with RoB 2. Weighted means and pooled percentages were calculated for participant characteristics.
paper.findings: Twenty-three studies (874 players) were included, with 5 accelerated and 7 criterion-based protocols and 11 unclassified. Two studies used all three test batteries (strength, hop and movement quality), eight used two, twelve used one and one used none. Mean surgery-to-return-to-play times ranged from 3 to 8 months. Only one study reported a return rate (95% returned to the same professional level), two reported complications, and all nine studies reporting PROMs showed significant improvement.
paper.limitations: Heterogeneity in sample size, protocols and outcomes limited pooling, and long-term follow-up was lacking (mean follow-up ranged from 4 to 19.2 months). Most studies were retrospective, female players were under-represented, and the authors note the findings may not apply to other sports. Risk of bias was rated by a single reviewer, and the review did not assess the predictive value of any test.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians can see that strength, hop and movement-quality batteries are common, but no single battery or criteria set has been shown to predict safe return. Programs should set and record their own progression criteria, and test results should be interpreted alongside clinical examination and the athlete's history.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the review supports using multi-domain test batteries during rehabilitation, but it does not give validated thresholds or identify which tests predict on-field performance, so any cut-off has to come from the program itself.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the study reports mean surgery-to-return-to-play times of 3 to 8 months, but it reports return rates in only one study and complications in two, so it cannot be used to set a clearance date, a return-rate target or the claim that a specific test makes return safe.

records.sourceFile: Rehabilitation and return to sport testing after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction - Where are we 2022.pdf

paper.citation: Gokeler A, Dingenen B, Hewett TE. Rehabilitation and Return to Sport Testing After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: Where Are We in 2022? Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2022;4(1):e77-e82.
paper.abstract: Athletes after ACL reconstruction often aim to return to preinjury sport, but few do, and second ACL injury rates are high after return. This clinical commentary reviews the current literature on RTS testing after ACL reconstruction and concludes that the validity of RTS criteria remains uncertain.
paper.tldr: Current return-to-sport test batteries after ACL reconstruction have uncertain validity, and common cut-offs such as a 90% limb symmetry index do not capture knee function. Staff should treat a passed test battery as one input to a clinical decision, not as clearance on its own.
paper.methods: Clinical commentary giving a critical overview of the literature on RTS testing after ACL reconstruction. The paper describes no systematic search, and its evidence is drawn from the cited studies and meta-analyses. Sections cover strength, hop tests, movement quality, psychological factors, rehabilitation approach, timing and consequences of testing.
paper.findings: The authors cite a meta-analysis in which only 23% of patients passed RTS test batteries before return, and report that passing criteria reduced subsequent graft rupture risk by 60% but raised contralateral rupture risk by 235%. Only 14% of patients reached an LSI of 100% for strength at two years, and 60% of patients showed abnormal landing kinematics even though 72.3% passed an LSI above 90% on hop tests. A test battery with an 80% pass rate per test falls to 64% for two tests and 51% for three.
paper.limitations: The commentary offers a critical narrative rather than a formal evidence grade, and its key claims depend on the cited studies. The abstract's 40% second ACL injury rate for athletes under 20 differs from the body, which attributes the 40% figure to men's Australian football. Exposure to high-risk activity after testing is often unreported, so test validity cannot be judged fully from these studies.
paper.practicalImplications: Use a multi-domain battery (strength, hop and movement quality) but do not rely on a single limb symmetry cut-off, because a passed LSI can coexist with abnormal landing mechanics. Record the athlete's exposure after clearance, since the authors argue that second-injury risk depends on what athletes do after testing.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the commentary supports measuring absolute strength and movement quality as well as limb symmetry during rehabilitation, because symmetry can mask deficits in both limbs. It does not provide validated performance thresholds.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the paper shows that current RTS batteries have uncertain validity and that passing them does not reliably identify athletes at risk of second ACL injury. It cannot be used to set a specific LSI threshold, a clearance date or a required test pass rate as a standalone decision rule.

records.sourceFile: Return to Play After Shoulder        Instability Surgery in National Collegiate Athletic Association    Division   I   Intercollegiate Football Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Robins RJ, Daruwalla JH, Gamradt SC, et al. Return to Play After Shoulder Instability Surgery in National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I Intercollegiate Football Athletes. Am J Sports Med. 2017.
paper.abstract: Retrospective case series of 153 NCAA Division I football players with 177 shoulder instability surgeries from seven programs. Return to play was 85.4% after isolated arthroscopic surgery with no difference by repair type, and returning players played a larger share of games than before their injury.
paper.tldr: In Division I football players, about 85% of those who had arthroscopic shoulder stabilization without other procedures returned to play, and returners often played in a larger share of games than before injury. Starters and scholarship players returned most often.
paper.methods: Retrospective case series of athletes from seven Division I football programs in the Pac-12, ACC and SEC, covering the 2004-2013 seasons. Data included instability direction, type of surgery, time to resume play, and games played and depth-chart status before and after surgery. Return to play required clearance from medical and athletic training staff and a return to the roster, and chi-square and Fisher exact tests were used.
paper.findings: Of 177 procedures in 153 athletes, 168 were arthroscopic and 9 were open bone-block operations. Return to play was 85.4% after isolated arthroscopic surgery, with no significant difference by repair type (82.4% anterior, 92.9% posterior, 84.8% combined), and games played rose from 49.9% before injury to 71.5% after surgery (P < .0001). Among returners, 15.6% later had a shoulder injury causing missed practices or games and 10.3% had recurrent instability requiring reduction or revision surgery.
paper.limitations: Retrospective design with possible recall or exclusion bias, no control group, and games-played data missing for two of seven schools (only 142 players analyzed for that outcome). Open-surgery numbers were small (9), and instability episodes that did not need reduction or revision were not recorded. The authors state the results should not be used to judge recurrent instability, because return to play, depth chart and games played do not measure it.
paper.practicalImplications: For a collegiate football player with shoulder instability, surgery led to a high return rate in this series. Expect lower return odds for players who rarely played before injury (75.7%) and for non-scholarship players (65.5%), and discuss later shoulder problems, which affected 15.6% of returners, with 10.3% having recurrent instability needing reduction or revision.
paper.athleteDev: Players who returned often played a larger share of games and kept or improved their depth-chart role after surgery, which can serve as a benchmark when planning roles. The study has no control group, so it cannot show that surgery itself caused these changes.
paper.rtp: The series gives return-to-play rates after shoulder stabilization in collegiate football, with 85.4% returning after isolated arthroscopic surgery and 10.3% of returners having recurrent instability needing reduction or revision. It does not set safe timing or readiness criteria, and it missed milder instability episodes, so it is weak evidence for clearing an individual athlete.

records.sourceFile: Return to Play After Shoulder Stabilization –What If This Isn't Going Well.pdf

paper.citation: Rosenthal MD, Wellsandt M, Specht Z. Return to Play After Shoulder Stabilization: What If This Isn't Going Well? Oper Tech Sports Med. 2024:151134.
paper.abstract: Clinical review of return to play after shoulder stabilization in athletes who are struggling to return. It covers the wide variation in return rates, the lag in performance after return to sport, and the impairments and interventions that may explain poor outcomes.
paper.tldr: Return to play after shoulder stabilization varies widely, and clearance by time alone misses impairments that matter. Rehabilitation should check range of motion, strength, neuromuscular control, kinetic chain mobility and psychological readiness before and during the return-to-sport progression.
paper.methods: Clinical review chapter. No systematic search or appraisal method is described. The chapter draws on published consensus statements, rehabilitation guidelines, return-to-sport studies and assessment methods, and sets out a phased framework with assessment techniques and exercise examples.
paper.findings: The chapter reports return-to-sport rates of 63% to 100% after stabilization, with performance lagging return to sport by 6% to 25%, most in throwing athletes. Time was the sole clearance criterion in 75% of studies it cites. It reports that athletes who did not undergo criterion-based return-to-sport testing were 4.85 times as likely to have recurrent instability after return, with a 22% recurrence rate versus 5% for those required to pass it.
paper.limitations: Narrative review with no described search or appraisal method. Several thresholds it presents come from studies of throwers and swimmers, and the chapter itself notes there is no consensus on return-to-play criteria or on the use of ER/IR ratios in collision sports.
paper.practicalImplications: Base the return-to-play decision on a test battery that covers range of motion (including total rotation arc asymmetry above 5 degrees in throwers), strength and endurance, neuromuscular control, kinetic chain mobility and psychological readiness, rather than time since surgery alone. Track workload with the acute:chronic ratio, while noting that the chapter's sources link ratios above 1.3 to injury in swimmers and overhead throwers.
paper.athleteDev: Returning to sport does not mean returning to performance. The chapter reports that performance lags return to sport by 6% to 25%, so staff should track strength, rate of force development, endurance and workload through the advanced phase, not only clearance.
paper.rtp: Clearance by time alone is not enough. The chapter recommends criterion-based return-to-sport testing and reports that athletes who did not undergo it had more recurrent instability. It gives reference thresholds rather than validated pass or fail cut-offs, so it cannot clear an individual athlete by itself.

records.sourceFile: Return to Play and Decreased         Performance After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in    National      Football League Defensive Players.pdf

paper.citation: Read CR, Aune KT, Cain EL Jr, Fleisig GS. Return to Play and Decreased Performance After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in National Football League Defensive Players. Am J Sports Med. 2017;45(8):1815-1821.
paper.abstract: Matched case-control and cohort study of 38 NFL defensive players after ACL reconstruction, compared with 38 matched controls. Players who returned were above-average before injury and were about average after returning, and fewer than two-thirds returned for at least half a season.
paper.tldr: About 61% of NFL defensive players who had ACL reconstruction returned for at least half a season, and those who did were above-average players before injury. After returning, their starts and solo tackles fell to about the level of average players, so counseling should cover both return and performance.
paper.methods: Retrospective matched case-control and cohort study. Defensive players with ACL reconstruction from 2006 to 2012, identified from public injury reports, were matched to controls on position and years of NFL experience, with performance statistics taken from the NFL database for seasons before and after injury. Successful return was defined as at least 8 games after surgery, and analyses used t tests, chi-squared tests, repeated-measures ANOVA and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis.
paper.findings: Of 38 injured players, 74% (28/38) played at least one NFL game after surgery and 61% (23/38) played at least 8 games. Before injury, returners started more games (80.9% vs 52.3% for non-returners) and made more solo tackles per game (3.44 vs 1.77) than non-returners, and after surgery their starts fell to 57.0% and solo tackles to 2.38 per game while matched controls did not decline significantly. Returners also showed a trend toward earlier retirement that did not reach significance (P = .064).
paper.limitations: The retrospective design relies on public media and the NFL database, so some injuries may be missed, and concomitant injuries, graft type, technique and rehabilitation were not recorded; position subgroups were small and no multivariable adjustment was made. The abstract describes retirement as significantly sooner and more frequent, but the results give P = .064. The abstract's comparison values do not match the tables (non-returners 54% starts and 1.82 solo tackles vs Table 1 52.3% and 1.77; controls 52% and 1.77 vs Table 3 60.5% and 2.50), and the table values are reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: In preoperative counseling, expect that about 6 in 10 NFL defensive players will return for at least half a season. Players who started often before injury were the most likely to return, and those who do return may not keep their pre-injury share of starts or tackles, so expectations for role and production should be set accordingly.
paper.athleteDev: Track games started and solo tackles through the first seasons after surgery, since returners declined on both while matched controls did not. In position subgroups, defensive backs significantly lost starts and interceptions, but these subgroups were small (only 3 linemen returned), so position-specific planning rests on thin data.
paper.rtp: The study gives return rates (61% played 8 games) and the timing of return (mean 47.0 weeks after surgery, range 29 to 101 weeks), but it cannot set readiness criteria or safe loading. It has no rehabilitation, graft or concomitant injury data, so it cannot guide the clearance decision for an individual athlete.

records.sourceFile: Return to Sport After Distal Biceps Tendon Repair - A Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Boufadel P, Daher M, Lopez R, Fares MY, Lawand J, Khan AZ, et al. Return to Sport After Distal Biceps Tendon Repair: A Systematic Review. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025.
paper.abstract: This systematic review pooled 42 clinical studies (1,093 patients) of distal biceps tendon repair to estimate return to sport, functional outcomes and complications. The overall return-to-sport rate was 91.5% at a mean of 6.3 months, and athletes alone returned at 96.4%.
paper.tldr: Most patients return to sport after distal biceps tendon repair, at a pooled rate of 91.5% around six months. Athletes returned at a similar rate of 96.4%, but took a mean of 9.4 months.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review of PubMed, Embase and Google Scholar, searched to December 2023, for clinical studies reporting return to sport after distal biceps repair. Two reviewers screened the studies independently, and outcomes were summarized descriptively in Stata across incision, fixation and rehabilitation groups.
paper.findings: The overall return-to-sport rate was 91.5%, and 506 of 594 patients (85.2%) returned to preinjury level or higher. Athletes had a return rate of 96.4% at a mean of 9.4 months. Complications occurred in 19.2% of patients, most often sensory neurapraxia, and 2.2% needed reoperation. Bone tunnel fixation, two weeks of immobilization and early active motion were associated with higher return rates, but only as trends in pooled data.
paper.limitations: All studies were level 3 or 4 evidence, outcome measures and protocols varied widely, and many studies did not report time to return. Incision, fixation and rehabilitation comparisons were not formally tested. The sample was 99.2% male and only 15.5% athletes, so the pooled rate is mainly a patient estimate.
paper.practicalImplications: Injured athletes can be told that return to sport after distal biceps repair is common, at about six months across the pooled sample and about nine months in athletes. Fear of rerupture and poor mental health were reported as reasons some patients did not return, so these should be discussed during rehabilitation.
paper.athleteDev: The review gives a realistic timeline for athletes who rely on elbow flexion and forearm supination, but it reports no strength or performance benchmarks, so training targets need other sources.
paper.rtp: Athletes returned in 96.4% of cases at a mean of 9.4 months, and early active motion and bone tunnel fixation showed trends toward higher return rates. These trends were not tested statistically, so they cannot justify choosing one protocol over another.

records.sourceFile: Return to Sport, Reinjury Rate, and Tissue Changes after Muscle Strain Injury - A Narrative Review.pdf

paper.citation: Wulf MW, Mackey AL, Kjær M, Bayer ML. Return to Sport, Reinjury Rate, and Tissue Changes after Muscle Strain Injury: A Narrative Review. Translational Sports Medicine. 2024;2024:Article 2336376.
paper.abstract: This narrative review examines how resistance training in rehabilitation affects return to sport, reinjury rate and tissue changes after acute muscle strain. Across the studies, mean time to return ranged from 15 to 86 days and reinjury from 0% to 70%, and structural changes appeared to persist after injury.
paper.tldr: Eccentric work at long muscle lengths and an early start to rehabilitation shortened return time in some trials. Reinjury rates varied widely, and the muscle and tendon changes after a strain may not fully resolve.
paper.methods: Narrative review of randomized controlled trials that included a resistance training component in strain rehabilitation, and observational studies of tissue morphology after muscle strain. No systematic search strategy is described.
paper.findings: Mean time to return to sport ranged from 15 to 86 days across eight studies, and mean reinjury rates from 0% to 70%. In the Askling studies, the long-length eccentric protocol reduced time to return by 45% and 38%, with low reinjury in all groups. In Bayer et al., early rehabilitation (day two) returned athletes in 63 days versus 83 days for delayed rehabilitation (day nine), with no difference in strength or muscle mass at return. Several other trials found no difference in return time between programs. Imaging-based injury severity was linked to longer return time in some studies, and muscle atrophy and aponeurosis changes were reported to persist for months to years.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative with no described search method, and the sample is largely hamstring strains in young athletes (mean age about 25). Trials differed in return-to-sport criteria, injury grading and follow-up length, and most had small samples, so their findings are not directly comparable.
paper.practicalImplications: For acute hamstring or calf strains, staff can start rehabilitation early and include eccentric work at long muscle lengths, which these studies associate with shorter return time. Return dates should be treated as individual, since the cross-study range was wide and reinjury risk did not always fall as return time lengthened.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Eccentric loading at long muscle length is the element the review supports most strongly for rebuilding hamstring capacity after strain, but it gives no sprint, power or load targets for the return phase.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Early rehabilitation start and long-length eccentric work were linked to shorter time to return in some trials, but the review cannot predict an individual return date from injury severity. The authors note a gap between subjective readiness, physical tests and tissue state at return, so clearance should not be read as full tissue recovery.

records.sourceFile: Return to Sport-Specific     Performance After Primary Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction A     Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Mohtadi NG, Chan DS. Return to Sport-Specific Performance After Primary Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Systematic Review. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2017.
paper.abstract: This systematic review identified 15 prognostic studies of sport-specific performance after primary ACL reconstruction in competitive athletes and rated their risk of bias. Most high-level athletes returned to sport, the bulk of evidence showed a measurable decline in performance statistics that was highly sport-specific, and the literature was judged highly biased.
paper.tldr: Many elite athletes return to sport after ACL reconstruction, but performance data are sparse, sport-specific and mostly biased. Expect a possible performance decline, not a fixed figure.
paper.methods: Systematic review of Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane databases and PubMed, with hand searching of reference lists, for prognostic studies of sport-specific performance after primary ACL reconstruction. Two authors independently selected and extracted the studies, and each was rated on six QUIPS bias domains, with the overall rating based on participation, prognostic factor and confounding domains.
paper.findings: Return to sport ranged from 63% (NFL players) to 97% (NHL players) across studies. Most studies reported no change or a decline in performance statistics after reconstruction, while three reported better performance in the ACLR group than in controls (hockey, soccer and alpine skiing). Most control-group comparisons favored the controls, but many lacked the numbers to show a difference and few corrected for multiple testing. Twelve of 15 studies were rated high risk of bias, mostly for how athletes were identified, and the two NHL studies reached different return and performance results depending on how injured players were found.
paper.limitations: Only high-performance or professional athletes were studied, and no meta-analysis was possible because the outcomes and performance measures varied by sport. Most studies were small, did not correct for multiple testing, and used a case-control design that is closer to a retrospective cohort. Non-returning athletes were not measured, so performance among returners may be overstated.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff counseling athletes about ACL reconstruction can say that many elite athletes return to sport, but that measured performance after return has generally declined or not changed, with large variation by sport. Because the data are biased, performance expectations should be presented as uncertain rather than as a fixed number.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The review gives no performance benchmark for returning athletes, so programs can only use it to justify tracking sport-specific output before and after injury, which the authors themselves recommend.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Most high-performance athletes returned to sport after ACL reconstruction (63% to 97%), but the review cannot show whether returners reach preinjury performance, because non-returners were not measured and the studies are rated highly biased. Return to sport alone should not be treated as evidence of a return to preinjury performance.

records.sourceFile: Return to performance - Machine learning insights into how absence time following muscle injuries affects match running performance in LaLiga soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Pecci J, Sánchez-Trigo H, Mancha-Triguero D, Sañudo B, Reverte-Pagola G, del Ojo-López JJ, et al. Return to performance: machine learning insights into how absence time following muscle injuries affects match running performance in LaLiga soccer players. Biology of Sport. 2025;42(4):275-286.
paper.abstract: This retrospective study of 110 muscle injuries in LaLiga players examined how absence time relates to changes in match running performance, using regression and random forest models. Maximal speed was the variable most strongly associated with longer absence, with maximal acceleration and deceleration also affected, while sprint count was not related to absence time.
paper.tldr: Longer time out after a muscle injury goes with a larger drop in maximal speed, and to a lesser extent acceleration and braking, in match play. Sprint count did not follow absence time, so it should be checked regardless of how long a player was out.
paper.methods: Retrospective design using match external-load data from the 2022-2023 LaLiga season, comparing four pre-injury and four post-injury matches for 110 lower-limb muscle injuries in 90 male players. Pre- and post-injury differences were tested with paired t-tests or Wilcoxon tests, then Pearson correlations with absence time were calculated, and multiple linear regression and random forest models with SHAP values were fitted to absence time using an 80/20 train-test split.
paper.findings: Mean absence was 34.6 days (SD 27.9), with 51 hamstring injuries. Time played, total distance, maximal acceleration, maximal deceleration, maximal speed, sprint distance, relative sprint count and the composite index differed significantly after injury. Maximal speed fell by a mean of 0.48 km/h and showed the strongest correlation with absence (r = -0.355), followed by time played (r = -0.328) and maximal acceleration (r = -0.303). Test-set R2 was 0.348 for linear regression and 0.442 for random forest, and maximal speed was the top feature in both models. Relative sprint count showed the weakest relationship with absence time in both models (r = -0.149).
paper.limitations: The sample is 110 injuries from one season, with a small test set and modest explained variance, and the training-set linear model R2 was only 0.12. The design is observational, so absence time cannot be separated from injury severity, tendon involvement, age or playing role, and no correction for multiple testing is reported.
paper.practicalImplications: After a muscle injury with a longer absence, staff should expect larger drops in match maximal speed and acceleration, so return-to-play criteria should include specific tests of maximal speed and acceleration or braking before clearance. Sprint count did not track absence time, so it should be checked regardless of how long the player was out.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Players returning after longer absences tended to show larger losses of top speed and acceleration in matches, so reconditioning should include speed and acceleration work targeted at those outputs. The paper reports no load prescriptions, so volumes must come from elsewhere.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study supports checking maximal speed, acceleration and deceleration before return to play, with more emphasis on those tests after longer absences. It cannot set a return date or a performance threshold for an individual player, and the authors' recommendation to check sprinting regardless of absence time also applies.

records.sourceFile: Return to play after a hamstring strain injury - It is time to consider natural healing.pdf

paper.citation: Pieters D, Wezenbeek E, Schuermans J, Witvrouw E. Return to Play After a Hamstring Strain Injury: It is Time to Consider Natural Healing. Sports Medicine. 2021.
paper.abstract: This review argues that current return-to-play criteria for hamstring strain injury ignore biological healing time, since muscle and scar tissue are still immature when athletes return at 11 to 25 days. The authors propose a minimum of 4 weeks before return after grade 1 or 2 injuries, alongside a comprehensive functional test battery.
paper.tldr: Athletes are usually cleared for return to play within 2 to 3 weeks of a grade 1 or 2 hamstring strain, before the muscle and scar tissue are mature. The authors propose a minimum 4-week period alongside the usual functional tests.
paper.methods: Review article combining prior return-to-play reviews and consensus statements with a PubMed search (August 2020) for hamstring return-to-play studies, plus a search of reviews on muscle healing. The authors used the findings to describe muscle healing phases, the timing of collagen and adhesion maturation, survey data on return criteria, and imaging evidence.
paper.findings: Average return to play after grade 1 and 2 hamstring strains was 11 to 25 days across criteria studies. In a worldwide survey of 131 premier league football teams, absence of pain, strength, training load and functional tests were the most used criteria, with an 'other' category (including time and imaging) chosen by only 1 to 2%. Basic science reports that muscle regeneration peaks around 2 weeks, type III collagen dominates through 2 to 3 weeks, and a firm attachment between regenerated fibers and scar forms around day 21. One study found about 25% of re-injuries in the first week after return, all at the index location.
paper.limitations: The review is not a systematic synthesis of clinical outcomes, and the 4-week threshold has not been tested in trials. The healing timeline comes from basic science studies of muscle healing, and the authors acknowledge that the proposed minimum may be longer than needed for some grade 1 injuries. Individual healing variability and the role of tendon involvement are unresolved, and the review applies mainly to grade 1 and 2 injuries in football.
paper.practicalImplications: For grade 1 or 2 hamstring strains, staff can treat four weeks from injury as a minimum before clearance, and still apply the functional test battery. The authors suggest that a player who passes functional tests before 4 weeks should still wait, and that a player who fails them after 4 weeks needs further assessment.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The review gives no load, speed or strength targets for the return phase. Its main point for performance staff is that good functional test scores can come before tissue maturity, so early test success should not be read as tissue readiness.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review supports a 4-week minimum before clearance for grade 1 and 2 hamstring strains, combined with functional tests and an individual assessment. It cannot show that the 4-week rule reduces re-injury, because that outcome has not been tested, and it does not apply to intratendinous or higher-grade injuries.

records.sourceFile: Return to play after hamstring      injuries in football (soccer)- a worldwide Delphi procedure regarding      definition, medical criteria and decision-making.pdf

paper.citation: van der Horst N, Backx FJG, Goedhart EA, Huisstede BMA, on behalf of the HIPS-Delphi Group. Return to play after hamstring injuries in football (soccer): a worldwide Delphi procedure regarding definition, medical criteria and decision-making. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2017.
paper.abstract: This Delphi consensus study of 58 experts from FIFA Medical Centres of Excellence defined return to play after hamstring injury in football and agreed the medical criteria and decision-makers. The panel defined return to play as criteria-based medical clearance and mental readiness for full availability, and excluded MRI as a criterion.
paper.tldr: Expert consensus defines return to play after hamstring injury as criteria-based clearance plus mental readiness. The criteria include pain-free palpation and tests, field performance and psychological readiness, and MRI is excluded.
paper.methods: Delphi procedure with four online rounds between July 2015 and July 2016, using 58 experts selected from 28 FIFA Medical Centres of Excellence. Items were drawn from a prior systematic review, and consensus was defined as at least 70% agreement, with response rates of 84% to 93%.
paper.findings: The panel agreed that return to play means criteria-based medical clearance and mental readiness for full availability for match selection and/or full training. Agreed criteria were medical staff clearance, absence of pain on palpation, pain-free strength, flexibility and functional testing, similar hamstring flexibility (0% to 10% difference), field performance testing and psychological readiness; similar eccentric hamstring strength was added as a potential criterion only in round 4, with the panel still divided. Field tests with at least 70% agreement were repeated sprint ability (76%), deceleration drills (71%), single-leg bridge (71%) and position-specific GPS-targeted match rehabilitation (82%). The sports physician was made ultimately responsible for the medical decision, with the physiotherapist, fitness trainer, athlete and team coach consulted. MRI findings were excluded.
paper.limitations: The consensus is expert opinion and has not been validated against re-injury or return outcomes. The 70% threshold is a convention, eccentric strength was added only in the final round, and the panel was drawn from elite football centres. Apart from the flexibility range, the criteria have no cut-offs, and the authors note that opinions may change as new evidence appears.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians can use the agreed criteria, pain on palpation, strength and flexibility checks, field tests including repeated sprints, deceleration and position-specific match rehabilitation, and psychological readiness, with MRI excluded from the decision. Return should be a multidisciplinary decision led by the sports physician, with the athlete and coaching staff involved.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The panel's field tests (repeated sprint ability, deceleration drills, single-leg bridge and position-specific GPS-targeted match rehabilitation) give sport-specific checks of performance before full training. The consensus gives no pass thresholds for these tests.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The consensus defines return to play and lists the criteria clinicians should check, including pain on palpation, strength, flexibility, field tests, and psychological readiness, with MRI excluded. It is expert opinion without validated cut-offs, so it cannot show that following it lowers re-injury risk.

records.sourceFile: Return to play and career length after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction among Canadian professional football players.pdf

paper.citation: Longstaffe R, Leiter J, Gurney-Dunlop T, McCormack R, MacDonald P. Return to Play and Career Length After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Among Canadian Professional Football Players. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020.
paper.abstract: This retrospective study followed anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstructions in Canadian Football League players from two teams between 2002 and 2017. Most reconstructions used hamstring tendon autograft, and about 70 percent of players returned to play with a mean career of about 2.8 seasons after injury.
paper.tldr: Nearly 70 percent of Canadian professional football players in this series returned to play after ACL reconstruction, similar to NFL reports. A concomitant MCL injury was the only significant factor linked to not returning in the adjusted model.
paper.methods: Team physicians and head athletic trainers recorded ACL injuries from two CFL teams from 2002 to 2017, including position, graft and concomitant injuries. Return to play and career length came from public sources, and returning and non-returning players were compared with t tests and a binomial logistic regression.
paper.findings: Of 43 analysable injuries, 30 (69.8%) returned to play after a mean of 316 days. Returning players averaged 2.8 seasons (34.4 games) after injury, with preinjury career length similar between groups. Hamstring grafts were followed by return in 64.5% (20 of 31) and patellar tendon grafts in 87.5% (7 of 8), and graft type was not a significant predictor. Meniscal injury was linked to lower return (61.5% vs 82.4%) and shorter careers, but this was not significant.
paper.limitations: Small sample, with return and career data from public sources that may contain errors, and no control group of uninjured players. The raw return rates were almost the same with and without an MCL injury (70% vs 69.7% in Table 5), so the MCL odds ratio comes only from the adjusted model and has a very wide confidence interval (1.1 to 32.8). The Discussion gives 58.3% for early-season injuries, while the Results give 56.8% (25 of 44), and the subgroup analyses are underpowered.
paper.practicalImplications: In this small series, hamstring grafts did not show a lower chance of return than patellar tendon grafts, so graft choice should not be decided on return rates alone. A concomitant MCL injury was the only significant predictor of not returning in the adjusted model, and all 3 players with a grade III MCL injury did not return. More than half of the injuries occurred early in the season, which the authors suggest warrants study of prevention strategies.
paper.athleteDev: The 2.8-season average career after return gives performance staff a rough benchmark for long-term planning in professional football players. Early-season clustering of injuries (56.8% in the Results) supports closer attention to preseason readiness, but the study does not test any training programme.
paper.rtp: The 69.8% return rate and 316-day mean time to return can serve as a benchmark for professional football players, but they cannot predict an individual's outcome. A concomitant MCL injury lowered the odds of return in the adjusted model and should be considered when planning. The study cannot show that any graft is safer, and it does not measure on-field performance after return.

records.sourceFile: Return to play and performance after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in National Football League players.pdf

paper.citation: Mody KS, Fletcher AN, Akoh CC, Parekh SG. Return to Play and Performance After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in National Football League Players. Orthop J Sports Med. 2022;10(3):23259671221079637.
paper.abstract: This study compared return to play and performance after ACL reconstruction across positions in 312 NFL players injured between 2013 and 2018. Players played fewer games, started fewer games, and had lower approximate value and snap counts after injury, and only 28.5% remained in the league three years later.
paper.tldr: Only about half of NFL players in this database returned to play after ACL reconstruction, and fewer than one in three were still in the league three years later. Running backs, defensive linemen and linebackers showed the largest performance drops.
paper.methods: NFL players with ACL reconstruction from 2013 to 2018 were identified from the FantasyData injury database. Games, starts, snap counts and AV were taken from Pro Football Reference for three seasons before and after injury, and pre- and postinjury values were compared with Wilcoxon and Kruskal-Wallis tests, with percentage change used to compare positions.
paper.findings: Of 312 players, 174 (55.8%) returned to play, and 59 of 207 (28.5%) remained in the league three years after injury. Within three years, players averaged 8.7 games versus 13.7 before injury, 3.0 starts versus 8.3, an AV of 1.5 versus 4.3, and 259 snaps versus 619. Quarterbacks had the highest return rate (92.9% vs 53.7%) and the smallest AV decline (2% vs 50%), while running backs had the largest AV decline (90.5%); in pairwise tests only quarterbacks versus running backs differed significantly, and snap-count change did not differ across positions after correction (P=.1113).
paper.limitations: The sample relies on public databases with no uninjured comparison group. The performance analysis covers only the 135 players who returned, and the 3-year analysis includes only players who stayed in the league. The text reports a 55.4% return (173 of 312) and the abstract 55.8% (174), while Table 2 gives 51.3% at one year; quarterback return is 92.9% in the text but 10 of 14 (71.4%) in Table 2, so the figures should be checked against the tables.
paper.practicalImplications: For professional football players, an ACL injury was followed by fewer games, starts and snaps, and fewer players were still in the league three years later. Return planning should account for the chance that players will not regain their pre-injury workload. The study does not show that any rehabilitation approach changes these outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use the position-level declines in AV and snap count as a broad benchmark for the level of workload that returning players may reach. Only the quarterback versus running back difference in AV change was statistically significant, so the other position rankings are descriptive. The study does not measure training or conditioning inputs.
paper.rtp: The 55.8% return rate and the 12.4-month average time to return can inform expectations for NFL players, but the study cannot predict an individual player's return. It does not show whether a specific rehabilitation protocol improves return, so it should not be used alone to set a return-to-sport date or criteria.

records.sourceFile: Return to play and performance after surgical repair of distal biceps tendon ruptures in NFL athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Pagani NR, Leibman MI, Guss MS. Return to Play and Performance After Surgical Repair of Distal Biceps Tendon Ruptures in National Football League Athletes. Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery. 2020 (online pre-proof).
paper.abstract: This case series of NFL players treated surgically for distal biceps tendon rupture compared return to play, performance and career length with position-matched controls. Most players returned to at least one game, but careers and games per season were shorter than for controls, and performance scores were not significantly different.
paper.tldr: Most NFL players in this series returned to at least one game after surgical repair of a distal biceps rupture, but only 56% were still in the league at two years. In a small scored subgroup, returning players' performance scores did not differ significantly from matched peers.
paper.methods: NFL players who had surgical repair of a distal biceps tendon rupture from 1998 to 2017 were identified from public injury databases and cross-checked with team and player sources. Each case was matched to a control by position, age and experience, and performance scores per game were compared with paired t tests, with Kaplan-Meier survival using final game played as the endpoint.
paper.findings: Of 25 cases in 22 players, 21 (84%) returned to play, at a mean of 321 days, with 1-year and 2-year survival of 76% and 56%. Post-injury career length averaged 2.8 years versus 3.4 years for controls (P=0.049), and games per season averaged 11 versus 13 (P=0.02). Post-injury performance scores did not differ significantly from pre-injury or matched-control values in any position group, although defensive linemen fell from 3.2 to 2.4 points per game (P=0.06, n=9).
paper.limitations: The sample is small, relies on public data without injury severity, technique or rehabilitation details, and offensive linemen were excluded from performance scoring, so only 16 cases were scored. The authors note that the lower career and games findings are likely confounded by factors such as trades and coaching changes, and they judge the career-length difference unlikely to be clinically significant. Time to return depends heavily on when in the season the injury occurred.
paper.practicalImplications: Surgical repair in this series was followed by return to at least one NFL game in 84% of players, but not all returned, so players and staff should not assume a full return. Returning players' performance scores were not significantly different from matched peers, though the scored sample is too small to rule out a decline. Expectations about career length and games per season should be discussed with caution because of confounding.
paper.athleteDev: Returning players in this series played somewhat fewer games per season than matched controls (11 vs 13), but the authors say this finding is likely confounded. The performance comparison involved only 16 defensive players and showed a non-significant drop in defensive linemen, so it cannot confirm that pre-injury performance standards will be met.
paper.rtp: The 84% return to play and the mean of 321 days to return can inform expectations, though the authors note that time to return depends heavily on the point in the season when the injury occurred. The study does not identify rehabilitation protocols or predict an individual player's return, so it should not be used alone to set return criteria.

records.sourceFile: Return to play and re-injury rates in NCAA Division I football players following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction using hamstring autograft.pdf

paper.citation: Jeffers KW, Shah SA, Calvert DD, et al. Return to Play and Re-Injury Rates in NCAA Division I Football Players Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Using Hamstring Autograft. Arthroscopy: The Journal of Arthroscopic and Related Surgery. 2021 (online pre-proof).
paper.abstract: This retrospective case series followed NCAA Division I football players who had ACL reconstruction with quadrupled hamstring autograft at a single institution between 2001 and 2016. Most players returned to play, the re-injury rate was low, and most reported good knee function years later.
paper.tldr: Most NCAA Division I football players in this series returned to play after hamstring-graft ACL reconstruction, and few re-injured their knee. Mean Tegner-Lysholm scores were high at a follow-up of about eight years.
paper.methods: Medical records of male varsity football players who had quadrupled hamstring ACL reconstruction by one surgeon from 2001 to 2016 were reviewed. Return to play, re-injury and eligibility used were taken from institutional records, and a survey provided Tegner-Lysholm scores, with t tests used for comparisons.
paper.findings: Of 34 players, 29 (85.3%) returned to play after a mean of 318 days, and 2 of those 29 (6.9%) re-injured their knee, both running backs with direct-blow contact injuries. Players with eligibility remaining used 79.5% of it, and the mean Tegner-Lysholm score was 90.7 plus or minus 14.2 among 33 respondents. Players with multiligament injuries did not differ significantly from isolated ACL injuries in time to return (348 vs 273 days, P=0.709).
paper.limitations: The study is retrospective, has no comparison arm, and includes a heterogeneous group of positions in a small sample. The Abstract gives return times of 306 days for isolated ACL and 353 and 324 days for multiligament injuries, which differ from the Results (348 vs 273 days), so the Results were used here; the Discussion also calls the 85.3% return 'the following season' while Results count any return with a mean of 318 days.
paper.practicalImplications: In this series, hamstring autograft was followed by return to play in most players and a low re-injury rate, so it is a reasonable option to consider in collegiate football players. Because there was no comparison group, the study does not show that hamstring grafts are as safe as patellar tendon grafts. About one in four players needed a second procedure on the same knee, which should be part of counselling.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can expect many collegiate players to use most of their remaining eligibility after hamstring-graft reconstruction, with 25 of 30 eligible players playing again. The study does not measure strength or performance outcomes after return.
paper.rtp: The mean 318-day return (range 115 to 628 days) and the 85% return rate can inform expectations for collegiate football players after hamstring-graft reconstruction. Clearance was a joint athletic training staff and surgeon decision using criteria that included 80% isokinetic strength, so the timeline should not be transferred to other protocols without checking them.

records.sourceFile: Return to play and recurrence after calf muscle strain injuries in elite Australian football players.pdf

paper.citation: Green B, Lin M, McClelland JA, Semciw AI, Schache AG, Rotstein AH, et al. Return to Play and Recurrence After Calf Muscle Strain Injuries in Elite Australian Football Players. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020.
paper.abstract: This study used Australian Football League registry data on calf muscle strains to examine whether clinical and MRI findings were associated with time to return to play and with recurrence. A running-related mechanism and aponeurotic disruption on MRI were linked to longer return to play, while older age and prior calf or ankle injury were linked to recurrence, and index MRI findings were not.
paper.tldr: In elite Australian Football players, calf strains with aponeurotic disruption on MRI and running-related mechanisms took longer to return to play. Recurrence was better predicted by age and prior calf injury than by the index MRI.
paper.methods: Clinical and MRI data on 149 calf muscle strain injuries were collected in the AFL Soft Tissue Injury Registry from 2014 to 2017. Two blinded radiologists classified MRI findings, and return to play, functional progression and recurrence within two seasons were analysed using Kaplan-Meier curves, Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis tests, and Cox regression.
paper.findings: Injuries with severe AD took 31.3 plus or minus 12.6 days to return to play, compared with 19.4 plus or minus 10.8 days with no AD (P=.003). A running-related mechanism was associated with longer return across all injuries (adjusted HR 0.59, P=.02), and AD was associated with longer return for soleus injuries (adjusted HR 0.6, P=.025), but not for all calf strains once adjusted (P=.11). Older age (adjusted HR 1.1, P=.013) and a previous calf strain (adjusted HR 6.7, P=.002) were associated with recurrence, while index MRI findings were not.
paper.limitations: The study has no uninjured comparison group and relies on registry data, with club staff not blinded to MRI results. Recurrent injuries were few (35 overall, 19 early), so the recurrence and subgroup estimates are imprecise, and the mechanism categories overlap. The authors also note that MRI may miss some structural damage, so injuries without visible AD may still have longer recovery.
paper.practicalImplications: For soleus strains with visible aponeurotic disruption, and for calf strains with running-related mechanisms, planning should allow for a longer return to play than for injuries without these features. Players with a previous calf strain or older age may carry a higher risk of recurrence, which should shape rehabilitation and return planning. Index MRI findings alone should not be used to predict recurrence.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use the longer return-to-full-training times for soleus strains with AD to set expectations for training reintroduction. Older players and those with prior calf strains may warrant closer attention during return to running, but the study did not test any monitoring method.
paper.rtp: Mean return-to-play times were 19.4 days with no AD and 31.3 days with severe AD, with wide spread, so the figures are group benchmarks rather than individual predictions. The study does not validate functional criteria for clearance, and the timelines come from one league, so they should not be applied to other sports without checking.

records.sourceFile: Return to play following Achilles tendon rupture in NFL players based on position.pdf
