paper.citation: Barton D, Manoharan A, Khwaja A, Sorenson J, Taylor M. Return to Play Following Achilles Tendon Rupture in NFL Players Based on Position. Foot & Ankle Specialist. 2021.
paper.abstract: This retrospective cohort study examined return to play and pre- and post-injury performance in NFL skill-position and linebacker players after Achilles tendon rupture and repair. Just over half of the players returned to at least one game, with rates varying by position, and returning players had more pre-injury games than those who did not.
paper.tldr: About 57 percent of NFL skill-position and linebacker players in this series returned to at least one game after Achilles repair, with tight ends and linebackers highest and wide receivers and running backs lowest. Players who returned were more experienced before injury than those who did not.
paper.methods: NFL injury reports and team rosters from the 2009-2010 to 2015-2016 seasons were used to identify players with Achilles tendon rupture and primary repair. Return to play was defined as playing in at least one NFL game after repair, and each returning player was matched to a same-position control from the same team, with pre- and post-injury statistics compared using paired and unpaired t tests.
paper.findings: Of 63 players, 36 (57.1%) returned to play, with rates of 71% for tight ends, 70% for linebackers, 62% for defensive backs, 40% for running backs and 38% for wide receivers. Returning players had more career games than non-returners (78.3 vs 25.4 for offensive players, P=.0072; 93.6 vs 33.1 for defensive players, P=.0043). In the returning group, passes defended fell from 5.04 to 2.79 (P=.0306) and other categories showed no significant within-group change, while against controls the returning players had fewer receptions per game (P=.01), tackles (P=.0069) and passes defended (P=.0452).
paper.limitations: The study is retrospective and built from public data, with concomitant injuries and surgical technique not recorded and small position groups that limit comparisons; running backs could not be tested statistically. The authors state that returning players declined in all categories, but Table 3 shows only one significant within-group change, the abstract counts fumbles forced/recovered (P=.0751) as significant, and the Discussion says passes defended increased significantly when Table 3 shows a fall. The Discussion's RTP rate of 58% and its claim that tight ends had the longest time to return (14.33 months) differ from the Results (57% and 11.25 months).
paper.practicalImplications: Expected return after Achilles repair varies by position in this NFL series, with wide receivers and running backs returning less often, so position demands should be considered when counselling players. Players who returned had more career games and starts before injury, which suggests that established players had better odds of returning. The performance data are too small and inconsistent to say how much returning players decline.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use the reported position return rates and the mean 12.6-month return as broad benchmarks for players returning from Achilles repair. The performance comparisons are small and partly inconsistent with the text, and the study does not test any training programme.
paper.rtp: Use the position-specific return rates (38% to 71%) and the mean time to return of 12.6 months as group benchmarks, not individual predictions. The return criterion here was a single NFL game, and the study cannot show whether any rehabilitation or operative technique changes that outcome.

records.sourceFile: Return to play following isolated and combined anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction - 25 years of experience treating NFL athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Khair M, Riboh J, Solis J, Maurer J, Brown JB, Vandermeer RD, et al. Return to Play Following Isolated and Combined Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: 25+ Years of Experience Treating National Football League Athletes. Orthop J Sports Med. 2020;8(10):2325967120959004.
paper.abstract: This case series reports two surgeons' experience treating NFL players with ACL injuries over more than 25 years, using both the standard return-to-game-play definition and a broader return-to-previous-participation definition. Return to previous participation was higher than return to game play, and age 25 years or younger predicted success.
paper.tldr: Most NFL players in this single-centre series returned to their previous level of participation after ACL reconstruction, and the rate was higher than return-to-game-play figures from earlier series. Players aged 25 or younger were most likely to return.
paper.methods: Retrospective review of prospectively collected data on NFL roster players who had ACL reconstruction by one of two surgeons at one centre. Return to game play (one regular-season game) and return to previous participation (passing a dynamic functional assessment, at least six weeks of position-specific activity, clearance by the NFL physical, and return at the same level) were recorded, and univariate and multivariate logistic and linear regression were used to identify predictors.
paper.findings: Return to game play after primary reconstruction was 73% (27 of 37 knees), and return to previous participation was 87.8% (36 of 41 primary reconstructions). Age 25 years or younger predicted return to previous participation (adjusted OR 10.8, 95% CI 1.4 to 233, P=.02), with 96.2% of players in that group returning compared with 76.2% of older players. Offensive players (adjusted 1.18 more seasons, P=.009) and players drafted in rounds 1 to 4 (adjusted 1.48 more seasons, P=.008) played more seasons after surgery, and later ACL tears occurred in 12.8% (graft rupture 4.3%, contralateral 8.5%).
paper.limitations: This is a single-centre series with two surgeons who also made return decisions, which may introduce selection bias, and follow-up duration was not recorded. The revision and multiligament groups are very small. The abstract gives 47 players while the Results give 47 reconstructions in 43 players, and its overall game-return rate of 67.6% differs from Table 4 (29 of 43, 67.4%); the claimed lower return after revision or bicruciate-plus-collateral reconstruction is not significant in Table 3 (P=.999 and P=.32), the text calls the primary versus revision game-return difference significant although Table 4 gives P=.07, and offensive position did not reach significance for return in the multivariate model (P=.07).
paper.practicalImplications: For NFL players after ACL reconstruction, age 25 or younger was linked to returning to previous participation, and draft round and offensive position were linked to more seasons played after surgery, so these should be part of counselling. The return rate depends on the definition used, so clinicians should state which definition they are using when comparing outcomes. The study does not support a claim that revision reconstruction or multiligament surgery lowers return with any confidence.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use the 2.6-season average participation after surgery and the higher seasons played by higher draft picks and offensive players as context for long-term planning. The study does not measure strength, speed or other performance outcomes after return.
paper.rtp: The 73% return to game play and 87.8% return to previous participation can serve as group benchmarks for NFL players after primary ACL reconstruction, with the authors' broader definition counting players who returned to their previous level without playing in a game. The study does not show that any rehabilitation protocol changes these rates, and the outcomes come from one centre, so the figures should not be applied to other levels without checking.

records.sourceFile: Return to play following meniscus surgery.pdf

paper.citation: Brelin AM, Rue JP. Return to Play Following Meniscus Surgery. Clin Sports Med 2016;35:669-678.
paper.abstract: The article has no abstract. Its key points state that meniscectomy gives a faster return to play but carries degenerative risk, that meniscus repair should be performed when possible in young active athletes, that accelerated repair rehabilitation gives equivalent functional outcomes, and that meniscal allograft transplantation is a viable salvage option, with contact or collision sport return weighed carefully.
paper.tldr: Meniscectomy returns athletes to sport fastest, but repair and transplant preserve the knee at the cost of longer, staged rehabilitation. Repair is favoured in young active athletes when the tear allows it.
paper.methods: Narrative review. The authors summarise prior studies and tables and describe their institution's rehabilitation protocols for repair (Box 1) and transplant (Box 2). No literature search method is reported.
paper.findings: Partial lateral meniscectomy returned 98% of 41 athletes to sport at an average of 55 days in one early series, and four NFL players who had midseason lateral meniscectomy returned at either 19 or 29 days. Accelerated repair protocols gave functional outcomes equivalent to standard regimens in the cited trials, and repair series report return to sport at roughly 5 to 6 months. In one allograft series, 10 of 13 athletes returned to their previous sport, with release to full training at about 4 months but a mean of 16.5 months to previous athletic level.
paper.limitations: The paper reports no search method and no pooled analysis. Most cited athlete series are small and differ in procedure, follow-up and return-to-sport definitions. The authors note there is little literature validating postoperative repair protocols, and the protocols shown are one institution's practice. The abstract is replaced here by the key points because none is printed.
paper.practicalImplications: Meniscectomy suits an in-season athlete who needs the fastest return, but the long-term osteoarthritis risk should be weighed and as much tissue as possible conserved. Repair is preferred in young, active athletes when the tear pattern allows, and accelerated rehabilitation can be used with the athletic trainer guiding progression. Allograft transplant is a salvage option, and the athlete should be told that return to collision or contact sport carries added risk.
paper.athleteDev: Use the surgery type to set the rehabilitation pace. The cited protocols return athletes to running and sport-specific work at about 6 weeks after meniscectomy and begin sport-specific and run/jump work at 16 weeks after repair. One cited repair protocol (Kozlowski and colleagues) advances athletes by criteria after a time-protected first 6 weeks.
paper.rtp: After meniscectomy, cited series report an average of 55 days to return to sport. After repair, roughly 5 to 6 months is typical in the cited series. After allograft transplant, full training at about 4 months does not mean return to previous level, which averaged 16.5 months. The review cannot set a clearance standard, because it describes no criteria-based testing and its cohorts are small.

records.sourceFile: Return to play practices following hamstring injury - A worldwide survey of 131 Premier League football teams.pdf

paper.citation: Dunlop G, Ardern CL, Andersen TE, et al. Return-to-Play Practices Following Hamstring Injury: A Worldwide Survey of 131 Premier League Football Teams. Sports Med 2020;50:829-840.
paper.abstract: Purpose: to determine whether premier-league teams worldwide follow a return-to-play (RTP) continuum, which criteria they use, and how decisions are made after hamstring injury. Methods: a structured online survey sent to practitioners at 310 professional teams from 34 premier leagues. Results: 131 teams responded (42%); 124 (95%) used a continuum assessing clinical, functional and psychological criteria, and 105 (80%) used shared decision-making. Team hierarchy, match and player factors were common perceived challenges. Conclusions: practice appears broadly consistent with general research recommendations, but specific criteria, metrics and thresholds, and the roles of staff in decisions, are unclear.
paper.tldr: Most professional football teams in this survey used a criteria-based return-to-play continuum with shared decisions after hamstring injury. The specific tests, metrics and thresholds they used were not clear, so the survey cannot show which ones work.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional online survey of 29 items (10 closed, 19 open) across four sections, adapted from a return-to-play continuum model. The survey was piloted for content validity, translated into six languages and sent to 310 teams from 34 leagues between October 2017 and March 2018, with up to three reminders. Open responses were analysed by content analysis, and two authors reviewed the coding.
paper.findings: 124 of 131 responding teams (95%) followed a return-to-play continuum, and 27 (21%) did not report a return-to-performance phase. Absence of pain, hamstring strength, training load and functional performance tests were the most frequently reported top criteria, and 68 teams (52%) reported always (100% of the time) meeting all their intended criteria before clearing players to high-speed running, with typical achievement of criteria at least 90% of the time. Medical staff were consulted at every phase, but the reported involvement of science staff, coaches and players depended on whether a medical or science practitioner answered the survey.
paper.limitations: Results are self-reported by 131 of 310 invited teams, so they may not represent non-responding clubs. The survey covers one muscle group and one sport, and it does not describe the metrics or thresholds used, or whether accelerated return led to re-injury. The authors classify the design as level 5 evidence and note that different staff roles gave different accounts of involvement.
paper.practicalImplications: Teams can use a criteria-based continuum with a shared decision, which the survey shows is common practice. Because the survey found no consistent metrics or thresholds, each team should define and record its own criteria and cut-offs. The survey also suggests the medical and science staff should agree on who is involved in each decision.
paper.athleteDev: Set progression criteria for each phase (running, team training, match play, return to performance) and track whether they are met. The survey shows training load and functional tests are commonly used, so build a training-load plan into the progression, but no specific thresholds are supported by this study.
paper.rtp: The survey describes how professional teams make return-to-play decisions after hamstring injury, including a continuum and shared decisions. It cannot show that these criteria or thresholds reduce re-injury, and it cannot be used to set a clearance standard for other muscle groups or injuries.

records.sourceFile: Return to sport after anterior cruciate ligament injury - Panther symposium ACL injury return to sport consensus group.pdf

paper.citation: Meredith SJ, Rauer T, Chmielewski TL, et al. Return to Sport After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: Panther Symposium ACL Injury Return to Sport Consensus Group. Orthop J Sports Med 2020;8(6):2325967120930829.
paper.abstract: Background: a precise and consistent definition of return to sport (RTS) after ACL injury is lacking. Purpose: to define RTS, describe the RTS continuum and give guidance on RTS testing and decisions. Study design: consensus statement. Methods: an international multidisciplinary group used a modified Delphi method, with a literature review. Results: RTS is achieved when the preinjury level of sport is reached, through criteria-based progression from return to participation to RTS and return to performance. Purely time-based decisions should be abandoned; decisions should be made by a multidisciplinary group using objective examination data and validated, peer-reviewed RTS tests that include functional and psychological assessment, and should consider biological healing, context and concomitant injuries. Conclusion: research is needed on the ideal test battery, psychological readiness testing and biological assessment of healing.
paper.tldr: Return to sport after ACL injury should mean regaining the preinjury level of sport, reached through criteria-based stages. Time alone should not decide clearance, and the decision should use examination data, validated tests and psychological readiness.
paper.methods: International consensus group of 26 ACL experts convened at a symposium in June 2019. A modified Delphi process ran three rounds (internet survey, structured in-person discussion and a final vote), with 80% agreement set in advance as consensus. Two liaisons completed a MEDLINE search (June 2019; anterior cruciate ligament, return to sport and return to play; 5 to 10 years) to support the statements.
paper.findings: Consensus was reached on 11 statements. Return to sport was defined as the preinjury level of sport (24 of 26, 92%), and purely time-based decisions should be abandoned (26 of 26). Objective physical examination was required (26 of 26), with validated tests (23 of 26) and a validated psychological readiness scale (22 of 26). Cited data from the Delaware-Oslo cohort show that patients who passed a criteria-based test at 6 months returned to their previous level at 81% (1 year) and 84% (2 years).
paper.limitations: The statements are consensus opinion built from an expert panel and a single MEDLINE search, not a systematic review or meta-analysis. The authors note that the best test battery, the psychological tools to use, and how to assess biological healing are not yet known. Some statements, such as the role of the coach, did not reach consensus, and the cited RTS outcomes come mainly from one cohort.
paper.practicalImplications: Use criteria-based progression through return to participation, return to sport and return to performance, with a documented clearance by the health care provider before unrestricted training. Include objective examination, a validated test battery and a psychological readiness measure, and consider contextual factors such as position, sport and concomitant injury. Avoid clearing an athlete on time alone, and treat RTS before about 6 months as likely high risk.
paper.athleteDev: Apply the RTS continuum to sport-specific training: clear unrestricted training first, then full participation in practice, then competition, with serial testing at each stage. Measure readiness with objective tests of strength, hop and movement quality before progressing, and do not use the calendar as the trigger.
paper.rtp: The statements describe a criteria-based return to sport after ACL injury, requiring objective examination, a validated test battery and psychological readiness, with time used as a guide to graft healing rather than the decision. The paper cannot specify the exact test battery or thresholds, and it cannot be used as a validated clearance protocol or as a guarantee of return to the preinjury level.

records.sourceFile: Return to sport and beyond following intramuscular tendon hamstring injury - A case report of an English Premier League football players.pdf

paper.citation: Taberner M, O'Keefe J, Dunn A, Cohen DD. Return to sport and beyond following intramuscular tendon hamstring injury: A case report of an English Premier League football player. Physical Therapy in Sport 2022;56:38-47.
paper.abstract: Background: hamstring strains are the most common injury in elite football and carry a high reinjury risk, especially when the intramuscular tendon (IMT) is involved, and rehabilitation data for these injuries are limited. Case scenario: an elite player suffered a grade 2c hamstring injury in an EPL match and was managed with early care, progressive off-pitch physical preparation and the control-chaos continuum for on-pitch rehabilitation, with objective and subjective load-response monitoring. Outcomes: on-pitch rehabilitation at 11 days, full team training at 35 days, match play at 40 days, and no reinjury for the rest of the season. Conclusion: knowledge of the IMT and expected return timeframes, with performance and load-response monitoring, communication and practitioner experience, may help to guide return to sport.
paper.tldr: A single elite player with an intramuscular tendon hamstring injury returned to full team training at 35 days and played at 40 days without reinjury. Isometric strength monitoring and load tracking guided each step, but this is one case.
paper.methods: Single case report of one 23-year-old male player managed by the club's medical and sports science staff. Care followed a modified return-to-sport continuum with the control-chaos continuum for on-pitch work. Isometric posterior chain peak force (unilateral test on a force platform at 1000 Hz) and interlimb asymmetry were measured weekly and before most training sessions. GPS load and MRI and ultrasound were used at set points, and the player gave informed consent.
paper.findings: Interlimb asymmetry in isometric posterior chain peak force fell below 10% by day 11, and the player reached his pre-injury weekly running load before full team training at day 35. He then played as a substitute for about 40 to 45 minutes in five matches and started one 90-minute match, where his high-speed running was 1.26 times his typical pre-injury game load, with no reinjury for the rest of the season. Authors note that the largest force decline came about 48 hours after match play, and it was symmetrical across both limbs.
paper.limitations: Findings come from one player, one club and one injury, without a control group. The authors state that the injury presentation, loading progressions, response to load and return timeframes are player-specific and may not transfer to other elite footballers, and that partial team integration may not always be feasible. The case cannot show whether the monitoring reduced reinjury risk.
paper.practicalImplications: Use an isometric strength test and load data before each stage of return, and combine them with pain response and player feedback. Consider an early phase of controlled loading and partial team involvement, as the authors describe, but expect the timeline to vary by injury and player. Keep monitoring after return to play, since the authors judged the reinjury risk after this injury type to be high.
paper.athleteDev: Use the control-chaos continuum to build back to match demands: progress high-speed running and maximal speed exposure against the match demand, and check strength asymmetry the morning after sessions. The case suggests that matching training volume to the player's pre-injury weekly running load was a practical target before full team training.
paper.rtp: The case describes one player who returned to team training at 35 days and to match play at 40 days after an intramuscular tendon hamstring injury, without reinjury for the season. It cannot set a return-to-play timeline for this injury, because the authors recommend an individual approach and the case involves no comparison.

records.sourceFile: Return to the pre-injury level of sport after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction - A practical review with medical recommendations.pdf

paper.citation: Solie BS, Tollefson LV, Doney CP, O'Keefe JMJ, Thompson WC, LaPrade RF. Return to the Pre-Injury Level of Sport after Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Practical Review with Medical Recommendations. Int J Sports Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: Return to sport after ACL reconstruction is complex, with return to the pre-injury level observed to be below athlete expectations and knee re-injury rates remaining high. The authors review graft, rehabilitation, objective testing, and psychological readiness factors and make medical recommendations for rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions.
paper.tldr: Return to pre-injury sport after ACL reconstruction varies widely by league, position and graft, and the authors recommend bone-patellar tendon-bone grafts for high-demand athletes, prehabilitation, a structured return-to-sport program, and repeated testing with psychological screening. Single test criteria should not be treated as proof of safe return.
paper.methods: A practical review of 158 unique articles found in Google Scholar, Medline and SPORTDiscus (June to November 2023), with at least two authors screening titles, abstracts and full texts and with reference checking. The search was not conducted to PRISMA or scoping-review standards, and each author was assigned writing sections based on clinical expertise.
paper.findings: Reported return to pre-injury level of sport varied by cohort, including 97% in the NHL, 80% in MLB, 77% in MLS, 92% in NFL quarterbacks, 86% in the NBA, 64.3% for NFL linemen and 69.5% in the WNBA. In a cited cohort, a BPTB autograft gave a higher return rate than a hamstring autograft (74% vs 53%), and an ACL plus MCL reconstruction gave 10% return against 48.9% after isolated ACLR (Svantesson et al.). Only 17% of athletes after ACLR, and 24% of non-injured athletes, met a 90% between-limb symmetry standard on a return-to-sport test battery, and the authors conclude that current criteria do not appear valid for predicting safe return.
paper.limitations: The review has no formal risk-of-bias appraisal and was not conducted to PRISMA or scoping-review standards. Most included evidence comes from retrospective or registry cohorts, outcome definitions differ across studies, and several medical recommendations rest on expert judgement rather than direct comparative trials.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the return rates as league-specific context rather than a prediction for an individual athlete, and treat passing a test battery as one input to a shared decision. The authors recommend prehabilitation, a comprehensive rehabilitation program, quadriceps strength and hop testing, ACL-RSI psychological screening, and a return-to-sport program before unrestricted participation.
paper.athleteDev: For athletes returning to high-demand sport, the review supports tracking quadriceps strength, hop performance and ACL-RSI scores through rehabilitation and before clearance. Performance staff should not assume a passed test battery means a safe return, and should keep secondary injury-reduction work in place throughout.
paper.rtp: The review can inform return-to-sport planning, including graft and concomitant-injury considerations, test selection and psychological readiness. It does not establish a validated clearance threshold, and it cannot tell staff what minimum time frame or test score makes return safe for a specific athlete.

records.sourceFile: Return-to-Play and Performance Outcomes of Professional Athletes in North America After Hip Arthroscopy From 1999 to 2016.pdf

paper.citation: Schallmo MS, Fitzpatrick TH, Yancey HB, Marquez-Lara A, Luo TD, Stubbs AJ. Return-to-Play and Performance Outcomes of Professional Athletes in North America After Hip Arthroscopy From 1999 to 2016. Am J Sports Med. 2018.
paper.abstract: Descriptive epidemiology study of 227 hip arthroscopy procedures in 180 professional MLB, NBA, NFL and NHL athletes from 1999 to 2016. Each player was compared with his own pre-surgery season, with return to play defined as at least one professional regular-season game.
paper.tldr: Most professional athletes in this public-source cohort returned to at least one game after hip arthroscopy, but performance and playing time often fell in the following season. Hockey players returned most often and quickest but showed the largest first-season performance drop.
paper.methods: Retrospective case identification from public sources (LexisNexis searches, player profiles, team reports and press releases), with at least two sources required per case. Each player was his own control, using the season before surgery as baseline, and performance scores were sport-specific (for example, player efficiency rating for basketball, on-base plus slugging for hitters, and position-specific formulas for NFL and NHL players). Comparisons across sports were adjusted for season and career length.
paper.findings: Return to play occurred in 84.6% of procedures (192/227). NHL players returned at 91.8% against 81.2% for other sports (P = .048), and NFL offensive linemen at 61.1% (P = .010), with mean return time of 209 days. Across the 170 players with performance data, performance scores fell 15.8% in postoperative season 1 (P = .022) and 14.4% in seasons 2 and 3 (P = .008). Only NHL players showed a significant season-1 drop (-35.1%, P = .002), and lead-leg MLB hitters showed a 12.7% reduction (P = .041). MLB pitchers who had surgery on their lead leg showed a 1.3% fall in fastball velocity (P = .004) and a 60.7% fall in pitch count in season 1 (P = .007), with both recovering by seasons 2 and 3.
paper.limitations: The authors state that a retrospective design, public-source capture and missing clinical data (imaging, rehabilitation, clearance, complications) limit interpretation. Revision and bilateral cases were pooled in the headline return rate, and sample sizes for individual sports and positions were small. The authors' hypothesis of consistently high performance return was only partly supported, because performance changes varied by sport and position.
paper.practicalImplications: When discussing return after hip arthroscopy with professional athletes, staff can expect high return rates in these leagues, but should also plan for lower playing time and performance in the first season, especially for hockey players. Positional demands, such as the lead-leg loading in baseball and the line play of NFL linemen, should be part of return planning. The authors also note that medical clearance does not equal game readiness, so game participation should be assessed separately.
paper.athleteDev: For professional athletes returning after hip arthroscopy, the study suggests tracking playing time, starts and sport-specific output across the first postoperative season rather than relying on return alone. The study's own findings show performance changes were not uniform across sports, so position-specific measures should inform progression.
paper.rtp: The study can support expectations for return to professional game play after hip arthroscopy in these four leagues, including the lower return rate for NFL offensive linemen. It cannot define a minimum time from surgery to safe return, because the dose-response analysis found no significant link between return time and performance change, and the study does not include clinical clearance criteria.

records.sourceFile: Return-to-Sport Rates and Functional Outcomes After Hip Arthroscopy for Femoroacetabular Impingement in Young Football Athletes - A 9.8-Year Follow-up.pdf

paper.citation: Schaefer JJ, Kang LS, Ward GH, Graden NR, Levy BA, Hevesi M, et al. Return-to-Sport Rates and Functional Outcomes After Hip Arthroscopy for Femoroacetabular Impingement in Young Football Athletes: A 9.8-Year Follow-up. Orthop J Sports Med. 2026;14(3).
paper.abstract: Case series of 36 hips in 27 young male football players who underwent primary hip arthroscopy with labral repair for femoroacetabular impingement, with a mean follow-up of 9.8 years. Return to sport and patient-reported outcomes were assessed, with 84% of players who returned to football at the same or higher level and significant improvements in all reported PROMs.
paper.tldr: Most young football players who attempted a return after hip arthroscopy with labral repair went back to competitive football at the same or higher level, with lasting improvements in hip scores. Non-medical reasons, such as graduation, accounted for many players who did not return.
paper.methods: Retrospective review of a prospectively maintained institutional database. Football players aged mostly under 25 with primary arthroscopic labral repair for FAI between 2010 and 2019 were contacted at least 5 years after surgery, and return to football, Modified Harris Hip Score, HOS-ADL, HOS-Sport, Tegner, VAS pain and satisfaction were collected. Predictors of return were examined with univariate logistic regression, and the authors note the sample was too small for formal power analysis.
paper.findings: Of 27 players (36 hips), 16 of 19 who attempted to return did so (84%) at the same or higher level, and the overall return rate was 16 of 27 (59%) after counting eight players who stopped for non-medical reasons. At a mean 9.8-year follow-up, mHHS improved from 68.5 to 90.5, HOS-ADL from 73.9 to 94.5 and HOS-Sport from 49.7 to 91.1 (all P less than .002 or .001). Two hips (8%) were reoperated, with no revisions, and no logistic regression predictor (BMI, age, level of play, alpha angle or position) of return reached significance.
paper.limitations: The study is a single-institution retrospective case series with no control group, and PROMs were available for only 19 of 27 players. The authors note that attrition (11 of 36 hips) and the small cohort may bias results, and that the predictor analysis was underpowered. The abstract gives reoperation as 2 patients (7%), whereas the results give 2 hips (8%); the figures differ because of the patient and hip denominators.
paper.practicalImplications: When counseling young football players about hip arthroscopy with labral repair, staff can share the favorable 5-year-plus function and satisfaction data, and should also discuss non-medical reasons such as graduation and changing priorities, which accounted for many non-returns. Clinicians should plan for a return rate below 84% when all players are counted.
paper.athleteDev: For young football players returning after hip arthroscopy, the study supports planned progression through the rehabilitation criteria (limb symmetry targets at week 12 and 16) before full football. Performance staff should also account for school and college transitions, since non-medical reasons drove most non-returns.
paper.rtp: The study shows that most players who attempted a return after labral repair went back to competitive football, but it cannot predict an individual's return, because no tested factor predicted return and the sample is small. It also cannot show that outcomes would match those in professional or older athletes, whose return rates were reported in other studies.

records.sourceFile: Return-to-play criteria following a hamstring injury in professional football - A scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: Perna P, Kerin F, Greig N, Beato M. Return-to-play criteria following a hamstring injury in professional football: a scoping review. Res Sports Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: Scoping review of the criteria used to determine return to play after a hamstring strain injury in professional male football. Four databases were searched, and 19 studies were included and grouped into clinical, strength and performance criteria, with clinical criteria further split into absence of pain, flexibility, medical clearance, psychological readiness, surgeon's opinion and imaging.
paper.tldr: Return-to-play after hamstring injury in professional football is guided by a mix of clinical, strength and performance criteria, but no criterion set has been validated. Staff should combine criteria in their battery and involve several disciplines in the decision.
paper.methods: Scoping review following PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-ScR, with a protocol registered on OSF in June 2023. Two reviewers screened PubMed, MEDLINE, Web of Science and SPORTDiscus records (1026 identified, 573 screened after duplicates removed, 19 included), and extracted design, sample, injury type and criteria. No risk-of-bias tool was applied.
paper.findings: Of the 19 studies, absence of pain was used as a criterion in seven, hamstring flexibility in five, psychological readiness in seven, strength in nine and performance in six. Imaging was a criterion in three studies, and the surgeon's opinion in one. One randomized trial (Tol et al.) found that 67% of players had at least one isokinetic deficit over 10% at return. MRI grade and the BAMIC classification were reported as predictors of time to return, with a 3-day rise in return time per BAMIC grade in one cohort.
paper.limitations: The review did not appraise study quality, and the authors note the evidence is weighted toward surveys, Delphi studies and case reports. Only English-language studies were included, and the review does not assess test validity or the optimal test for each injury type and stage. The text and flow diagram disagree on the number of full texts screened (52 vs 51).
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should use a combination of clinical, strength and performance criteria, and make the return decision with several disciplines involved. Strength testing should include hamstring isokinetic or isometric tests, and the authors note that the choice of test is not settled. Psychological readiness should be assessed, although no validated tool exists in this population.
paper.athleteDev: For professional footballers returning from hamstring injury, the review supports a criteria-based battery that includes absence of pain, hamstring strength and flexibility, sport-specific performance and load monitoring. Performance staff should plan for the high re-injury risk noted in the introduction, rather than relying on a single test.
paper.rtp: The review can inform the clinical, strength and performance criteria used in return-to-play planning after hamstring injury in professional football. It cannot be used to set a validated pass or fail threshold, and the authors state it does not provide clinical practice guidelines.
